title: Gross, operating, and net profit
subtitle: Three tiers of profit - each tells a different story
openingQuestion: What is the difference between Gross Profit, Operating Profit, and Net Income?
openingOptions: Gross Profit is always the largest
They're the same thing, just different names
Each tier deducts a different additional type of cost
explanation: The income statement peels profit into three tiers, and each one answers a different question. Gross profit tells you whether making the product is profitable. Operating profit tells you what's left after feeding the entire sales and admin machine. Net income tells you the final piece belonging to shareholders, after interest and tax. Reading all three is what reveals whether a problem sits in production, in operations, or in the capital structure.

diagram.label: Subtract cost of goods sold: left with gross profit
Subtract selling and admin expenses: left with operating profit
Subtract interest and tax: left with net profit

realWorldExample.description: Mobile World keeps a Gross Margin steady around 20%, but its Operating Margin swings much more depending on store rent and chain operating costs - a clear illustration of how the three profit tiers reflect different problems.

quiz.question: If company A's Operating Margin is 15% and company B's is 10%, what does that mean?
options: A earns 15 dong, B earns 10 dong, per 100 dong of revenue
A pays less interest and tax than B, so it ends up more profitable
A has revenue 1.5 times higher than company B
A's cost of goods sold is exactly 5 points lower than B's
quiz.explanation: Operating Margin shows operational efficiency before interest and tax. Company A has better operating efficiency, but Net Margin could still be lower if A carries more debt (higher interest expense).

quiz.question: A high Gross Margin but a low Operating Margin usually suggests what?
options: The company is pricing its products too high relative to the general market
Operating costs (SG&A, R&D) are too high relative to revenue, eating into the gross profit
Customers are increasingly reluctant to buy the company's products as before
The company is selling products at too low a price relative to its production costs
quiz.explanation: A high Gross Margin means the company sells goods profitably. But if operating costs (sales, admin, R&D) are large, operating profit gets eaten away. This is an operational-efficiency problem.

quiz.question: Company X's Net Income is 50m but its Operating Income is only 60m. What just happened?
options: The company spent 10m on selling and admin expenses
The company booked an extra 10m of cost of goods sold in the period
The company paid interest and tax, totalling 10m
The company lost 10m from its core business operations
quiz.explanation: Operating Income is profit before interest and tax (EBIT). Net Income comes after. The gap reflects interest expense (debt) and tax, not an operational problem.

quiz.question: Retailers typically have a Gross Margin around 25-30% and an Operating Margin around 5-10%. Where does this gap mainly come from?
options: The cost of goods sold in the retail industry is inherently very high
The tax rate applied to the retail industry is higher than other industries
Large interest expense because retail requires heavy working-capital borrowing
High SG&A costs: salaries, rent, marketing
quiz.explanation: Retail has a decent product margin but very large operating costs (thousands of stores, complex supply chains, marketing). SG&A eats away 15-20% of revenue.

quiz.question: How can you tell whether a problem sits in production or in operations?
options: Look at Gross Margin (a production/COGS issue) versus Operating Margin (an operational/SG&A issue)
Just looking at the company's total sales figure for the reporting period is enough to conclude
The only reliable way is to ask the company's CEO directly about the issue
There is no way whatsoever to distinguish between these two types of problems
quiz.explanation: If Gross Margin is poor and Operating Margin is also poor = a production/COGS problem. If Gross Margin is good but Operating Margin is poor = an operational/SG&A problem.

quiz.question: Company A has: GM=50%, OM=30%, NM=20%. Company B has: GM=40%, OM=30%, NM=15%. Compare the two.
options: The two companies are equal since equal OM is enough to conclude that
A is better at production, OM is equal, A is ahead at the net level
A is better operationally but weaker at the production stage
B is better overall since every margin of theirs is more stable
quiz.explanation: Different GM → A is better at production/COGS. Equal OM → operations are similar. Different NM → A has a better capital structure (less interest, lower tax).

quiz.question: If you're an investor, which profit metric matters to you most?
options: All three, since each tier tells you something different
Only Operating Margin, since it strips out financial noise
Only Gross Margin, since it reflects product strength
Only Net Margin, since it's the final number
quiz.explanation: Investors need to look at all three to clearly understand: is the company profitable from its core business (GM, OM), or does the profit come from unusual, one-off items (NM higher than OM)?

keyTakeaways: Gross Profit measures core production/business efficiency
Operating Income measures the efficiency of running the whole business
Net Income is the final figure after interest and tax

practicePrompt.question: Garment company X has a Gross Margin of 45% (very good for its industry) but an Operating Margin of only 4% (far below competitors' 10%). Where does company X's problem lie?
options: In operations - SG&A costs (sales, admin, marketing) are too high relative to revenue, eating up most of the strong gross profit already generated
In production - because a 45% Gross Margin shows the company producing less efficiently than its competitors
There's no problem at all since a 4% Operating Margin is still a positive figure - the company is still profitable
In paying too much interest on debt, since that's the only line item sitting between Gross Profit and Operating Income
practicePrompt.explanation: A high Gross Margin proves the production/COGS side is fine. The problem lies in the big gap between Gross Margin and Operating Margin - that gap is operating costs (SG&A) running too high, not yet a matter of interest expense (which sits below Operating Income).

summary.keyIdea: Gross Profit measures core production/business efficiency
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Operating Income measures the efficiency of running the whole business

application.title: Try computing the three profit tiers
application.message: Take the financial statements of a company you're interested in, find the Revenue, COGS, Operating Expenses, Interest, and Taxes lines, then recompute Gross Profit, Operating Profit and Net Income using the formulas from this lesson.
application.secondary: Compare your result against what the company publishes to check you understood correctly.

sections.text: Mobile World can announce 'profit' three different ways in the same report - and all three are correct, each just answering a different question. Without understanding these three tiers, investors easily get confused comparing companies against each other.

Gross Profit = Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). This is the first and most basic figure, measuring how much the business profits from selling its products/services before accounting for other operating costs like office staff salaries, marketing, or rent. Gross Margin = Gross Profit ÷ Revenue, showing what percentage of each dong of revenue is left after deducting direct production/purchasing costs.

Operating Profit = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses (including SG&A: sales, admin; and R&D if applicable). This figure reflects the efficiency of the entire core business operation, before accounting for capital structure (how much debt is used) or tax. This is the figure analysts most often use to compare operational efficiency between companies in the same industry, since it strips out the effect of how a company finances itself.

Net Income = Operating Profit − Interest Expense − Corporate Income Tax ± other one-off items. This is the 'final' figure - what truly belongs to shareholders after all obligations are settled, used to calculate EPS (earnings per share) and ROE.

items: Unusually low Gross Margin versus the industry → may come from weak pricing or rising raw material costs
High Gross Margin but low Operating Margin → operating costs (rent, advertising, staffing) are eating into profit
Good Operating Margin but low Net Margin → the company may carry heavy debt (high interest) or face an unfavourable tax rate
Net Income spiking in one quarter → check whether it came from a one-off item (asset sale, reversal of a provision) rather than core operations
